title: Docker
summary: Images, containers and how to build them securely.

cards.question: What is the difference between an image and a container?
cards.answer: An image is an immutable, read-only template made of layers. A container is a running instance of an image with an ephemeral writable layer on top.

cards.question: When do you use volumes and when bind mounts?
cards.answer: A container filesystem is ephemeral. Volumes are managed by Docker and are the way to persist data (for example a database). Bind mounts map a host path and are used in development to see code changes instantly.

cards.question: Why does instruction order matter in a Dockerfile?
cards.answer: Each instruction creates a cached layer; if one changes, all following ones are invalidated. Order from least to most changing: copy package.json and install dependencies first, then copy the source.

cards.question: What is a multi-stage build and what does it give you?
cards.answer: You use one stage with all build tools and copy only the output into a minimal final image. The image is smaller, pulls faster and exposes less attack surface.

cards.question: Which security measures do you apply to a production image?
cards.answer: Non-root user, minimal base image pinned by version or digest, no secrets inside layers (inject them at runtime), vulnerability scanning, read-only filesystem and dropped Linux capabilities.

cards.question: Why can a Node.js container be slow to stop with docker stop?
cards.answer: The main process is PID 1, which gets no default signal handling: SIGTERM may be ignored and Docker ends up sending SIGKILL after the timeout. Use exec-form CMD, an init such as tini (docker run --init) and a SIGTERM handler in the app.
